analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall separating insured bank deposits from securities trading.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 83 cosponsors from both parties, but the House Financial Services Committee never gave it a hearing or a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rebuild the Glass-Steagall separation, repealed in 1999, between commercial banks that hold government-insured deposits and securities firms that trade and underwrite stocks and bonds. Insured banks could no longer affiliate with broker-dealers, investment advisers, or investment companies, and securities-firm executives could no longer sit on bank boards. Existing combined firms would have two years, extendable by up to one more, to unwind those affiliations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers: money backed by federal deposit insurance would no longer sit inside companies also exposed to securities losses. Smaller commercial banks that never combined banking with securities would no longer compete against conglomerates with both advantages. The bill also tries to stop regulators from slowly eroding the new wall by locking in a strict Supreme Court reading and requiring a report to Congress for every exception granted.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors, taxpayers, and smaller commercial banks

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any insured depository institution from affiliating with a broker-dealer, investment adviser, investment company, or other securities firm, so government-insured deposits are no longer housed inside companies exposed to securities losses.

Bars officers, directors, and employees of securities firms from simultaneously serving on the boards of insured banks, with current dual-serving officials required to give up one post within 60 days.

Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that created financial holding companies combining banking with securities and insurance businesses, and requires those combinations to be unwound within two years, extendable up to one additional year.

Locks in the Supreme Court's strict reading of the banking-securities separation in Investment Company Institute v. Camp and forbids federal banking agencies or courts from interpreting the new limits more narrowly, with regulators required to report to Congress each time they grant an exception or extension.

analysis.who_pays: Universal banks that house insured deposits and securities businesses under one roof, along with their shareholders, would have to sell, spin off, or wind down their securities operations. Some customers would lose one-stop banking and brokerage services, and the forced divestitures could be disruptive while they happen.

drawbacks.text: Forcing large banking companies to unwind their securities affiliates within roughly two to three years would be a costly restructuring, and the upheaval could disrupt credit and financial services while it took place.

The bill hard-wires the strict Investment Company Institute v. Camp interpretation and prohibits any court or regulator from reading the separation more narrowly, leaving little flexibility for banks seeking approval for activities that might be safe.

Reinstating Glass-Steagall would not necessarily have prevented the 2008 crisis: the largest failures, such as Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns, were stand-alone securities firms that Glass-Steagall never covered, so the bill's protective value is genuinely debated among economists.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that government-insured deposits should not sit inside firms making bets on securities — addresses a real risk to taxpayers, and the bill's phased wind-down shows its authors tried to avoid a sudden shock. But the biggest 2008 collapses were securities firms outside the old wall, so reinstatement would have addressed part, not all, of the danger, and the forced breakups would carry real short-term costs. On balance, the bill would have traded a large, hard-to-measure stability gain for a large, measurable restructuring cost borne by the biggest banks.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to the Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, so the bill simply expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on January 3, 2013, joined by Republican Rep. Walter Jones as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services, which was the last action the bill ever received.
The bill attracted 83 cosponsors, 77 Democrats and 6 Republicans, but was never reported out of committee, never debated, and never voted on in either chamber.
It died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, with all work on the bill erased.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large universal banks that hold insured deposits and run securities businesses under one roof kept that structure intact for another two years, with no vote ever taken on separating them. The bipartisan 83-member coalition in the House got nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big universal banks that kept deposits and trading combined

for.name: Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 3, 2013, to restore the Glass-Steagall separation.

for.name: Walter Jones
for.what_they_did: Joined Kaptur in introducing the bill as its original Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; the record shows no committee action after referral for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority control of the House floor agenda
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote at any point in the 113th Congress.

against.name: Large universal banks and financial industry trade groups
against.role: Combined banking-securities firms affected by the bill
against.what_they_did: Opposed reinstating the Glass-Steagall separation, which would have forced them to break apart their banking and securities operations.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 77 of the 83 cosponsors were Democrats — though a small bipartisan group of 6 House Republicans and original cosponsor Walter Jones crossed over; opposition came from the Republican-run committee and House majority that never acted on it.

industries.industry: Universal banks and financial holding companies (e.g., firms combining commercial banking with securities)
industries.note: The bill would force them to divest or wind down securities affiliates within about two to three years, ending the structure in which government-insured deposits sit inside firms also exposed to securities losses. Their interest in keeping that structure runs against the taxpayer protection the bill offers.

industries.industry: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and investment companies affiliated with banks
industries.note: They would lose bank affiliations and their officers could no longer sit on insured-bank boards, cutting off the access to deposit-funded scale that Glass-Steagall's repeal gave them.

industries.industry: Smaller commercial banks without securities businesses
industries.note: These banks would no longer compete against conglomerates that can pair insured deposits with securities operations, leveling the competitive field. Their customers are the same depositors the bill aims to protect.
